segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Again he began to teach beside the sea. A very large crowd gathered around him, so that he got into a boat and sat in it on the sea, while the whole crowd was on the land, facing the sea.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He taught them many things in parables, and in his teaching he said to them:

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Listen! Look, a sower went out to sow.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And as he sowed, some seed fell along the path, and the birds came and ate it up.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Other seed fell on the rocky ground, where it did not have much soil, and it sprang up at once because it had no depth of soil.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And when the sun rose it was scorched, and because it had no root it withered.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Other seed fell among the thorns, and the thorns came up and choked it, and it yielded no crop.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And other seeds fell into the good soil and yielded a crop, coming up and growing, and bore thirtyfold and sixtyfold and a hundredfold.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Whoever has ears to hear, let them hear.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When he was alone, those around him, together with the Twelve, asked him about the parables.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “To you the secret of the kingdom of God has been given, but to those outside everything comes in parables,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: so that they may look and look yet not see, and hear and hear yet not understand; otherwise they might turn back and be forgiven.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “You do not understand this parable? Then how will you understand all the parables?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: The sower sows the word.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: These are the ones along the path, where the word is sown: when they hear it, Satan comes at once and takes away the word that was sown in them.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And these, likewise, are the ones sown on the rocky ground: when they hear the word, they at once receive it with joy,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: yet they have no root in themselves and last only for a time; then, when affliction or persecution comes because of the word, at once they fall away.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Others are the ones sown among the thorns: these are the ones who have heard the word,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: but the worries of the age, the deceitfulness of wealth, and the desires for everything else come in and choke the word, and it yields no crop.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And those are the ones sown on the good soil: they hear the word and welcome it and yield a crop, thirtyfold and sixtyfold and a hundredfold.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Does the lamp come to be put under the basket or under the bed? Does it not come to be put on the lampstand?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For nothing is hidden except to be disclosed, nor has anything been concealed except to come into the open.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: If anyone has ears to hear, let them hear.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Pay attention to what you hear. With the measure you measure with, it will be measured to you, and more will be added to you.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: For to the one who has, it will be given; and from the one who does not have, even what that person has will be taken away.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “The kingdom of God is like this: it is as if someone scatters seed on the earth

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: and sleeps and rises, night and day, and the seed sprouts and grows, though he himself does not know how.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: On its own the earth yields a crop: first the blade, then the ear, then the full grain in the ear.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But when the crop is ripe, at once he sends in the sickle, because the harvest has come.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “To what shall we compare the kingdom of God, or what parable shall we use for it?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: It is like a mustard seed, which, when it is sown on the earth, is smaller than all the seeds on the earth,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: yet when it is sown, it comes up and becomes larger than all the garden plants and puts out large branches, so that the birds of the sky can nest in its shade.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: With many such parables he spoke the word to them, as far as they were able to hear it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He did not speak to them without a parable, but in private he explained everything to his own disciples.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: On that day, when evening had come, he said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Let us cross over to the other side.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Leaving the crowd, they took him along in the boat, just as he was; and other boats were with him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: A great windstorm arose, and the waves were breaking into the boat, so that the boat was already filling.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But he was in the stern, asleep on the cushion. They woke him and said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Teacher, do you not care that we are perishing?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He woke up, rebuked the wind, and said to the sea,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Quiet! Be silent!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And the wind died down, and there was a great calm.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Why are you cowardly? Do you still have no faith?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And they were filled with great fear and said to one another,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Who then is this, that even the wind and the sea obey him?”

notes.note: Mark calls the freshwater Lake of Galilee a “sea,” following Semitic usage in which one word covers any large body of water. The rendering keeps “sea” because the storm scene that closes the chapter draws on Old Testament language about God mastering the sea.

In the Greek Old Testament this word translates a Hebrew term covering proverbs, riddles, taunts and extended comparisons. A first-century hearer would not have limited it to illustrative stories. The wider sense, including “riddle,” matters for verse 11, where everything comes “in parables” to outsiders.

In Jewish Greek of the period, notably the Greek book of Daniel, this word is the ordinary term for a secret, especially a plan of God that only he can disclose. English “mystery” now suggests a puzzle or something beyond understanding, which is not the point. Many versions keep “mystery” as an established term, though several (RSV, NRSV, NIV) also use “secret” in this saying.

The words echo Isaiah 6:9–10, in a form closer to the Aramaic synagogue paraphrase (“be forgiven”) than to the Hebrew or the Greek version (“be healed”). The conjunction normally expresses purpose, and many scholars read it so here: the parables carry out the judgment Isaiah announced on unresponsive hearers. Others take it as result (“with the result that”) or as shorthand for “so that Scripture is fulfilled,” and some read the last clause as “unless perhaps they turn.” The rendering keeps the plain purpose sense and does not resolve the difficulty.

The verb comes from the Greek Old Testament’s word for a trap or obstacle and means to be tripped up in one’s loyalty to God. The King James Version’s “are offended” now suggests hurt feelings, which is too weak for people who abandon the word under persecution. Most modern versions also have “fall away” here.

The Greek word is a time-word meaning an era, here the present age as contrasted with the age to come. “World” blurs this and suggests a different Greek word. Lexicons accept “age” here, though many versions keep “world.”

The Greek says literally that the lamp “comes,” with the definite article, and most versions smooth this to “is a lamp brought.” It may be no more than a loose idiom. Many interpreters, however, think the odd wording hints at the coming of Jesus or of the kingdom, hidden now but meant to be revealed, so the literal verb is kept.
The word names a household vessel for measuring grain, holding roughly two gallons (about nine liters). “Bushel,” the traditional rendering, is a much larger measure and now an unfamiliar one.

The verb normally means “hand over.” Here alone in the New Testament it is used of a crop, with no object. Most scholars take it to mean “permits,” that is, the crop is ready for harvest, and nearly all modern versions have “is ripe”; a few suggest “yields itself.”

notes.phrase: he sends in the sickle, because the harvest has come
notes.note: The wording echoes Joel 3:13, where sending in the sickle at harvest is a picture of God’s final judgment. A hearer who knew the prophets would have caught the reference, which gives the quiet growth of the seed a decisive end.

notes.phrase: the birds of the sky can nest in its shade
notes.note: The picture recalls the great tree of Ezekiel 17:23 and 31:6 and Daniel 4:12, in whose branches or shade the birds lodge. That tree is an image of a kingdom sheltering many peoples. Applying it to a garden shrub grown from a tiny seed is part of the parable’s point.

The second command uses a verb meaning literally “muzzle” and commonly “silence.” Jesus uses the same verb to silence an unclean spirit at Mark 1:25, and the narrator’s word “rebuked” appears in both scenes. The traditional “Peace! Be still!” is gentler than the Greek, which addresses the sea as a hostile power being shut up.

The Greek adjective means timid or cowardly and is a reproach. It is a different word from the “fear” of the next verse, which is closer to awe. Most versions use “afraid” or “fearful” for both, which hides the contrast between the cowardice Jesus rebukes and the great fear that follows the calm.

candidates.reason: Mark’s signature adverb occurs some forty times, and versions vary among “immediately,” “at once” and “straightway”; one rendering lets the reader hear the refrain.
“Fruit,” “grain” and “crop” are all defensible for a harvest; the choice affects whether the parable and its interpretation, and the wider “bear fruit” language, stay visibly linked.
Used of Jesus commanding demons, wind and disciples; a uniform rendering preserves the link between exorcisms and the stilling of the storm.
Versions vary among “turn,” “return,” “be converted” and “repent” for turning to God; it needs to be kept distinct from μετανοέω across the New Testament.
For the Lake of Galilee, versions alternate between “sea” and “lake”; a single decision is needed because Old Testament sea imagery depends on it.

warnings: Verse 29: παραδίδωμι is not rendered with a register form (hand over; hand on; hand down; give up; give over; entrust; risk; be ripe) and has no register-exception note.
